nameStory: The northern sennet gets its name from its northerly range compared to other barracudas, which are typically tropical fish. The word 'sennet' comes from an old nautical term for a type of braided rope, possibly referring to the fish's sleek, rope-like body shape that cuts through water.
description: The northern sennet is New England's only member of the barracuda family, bringing a taste of the tropics to our cooler waters. This silvery, torpedo-shaped fish has an elongated body built for speed, with a distinctive pointed snout filled with sharp teeth. Northern sennets typically reach 12-18 inches in length and have a streamlined appearance that makes them efficient ocean predators.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Long, slender torpedo shape with a firm, muscular feel when handled - built like a living arrow designed to slice through water

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Elongated, pointed snout with a large mouth filled with razor-sharp teeth that feel like tiny needles - handle with extreme care

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright silver sides that feel smooth and slightly slimy, with a darker blue-green back that creates excellent camouflage from above and below

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Two separate dorsal fins - the first small and spiny, the second larger and soft-rayed, positioned far back near the tail

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Medium-sized for New England waters at 12-18 inches, with a surprisingly solid, dense feel for their slender appearance

habitat: Northern sennets patrol the open waters off New England's coast, preferring the deeper offshore areas where they hunt in small schools. They're most commonly found in the warmer months when Gulf Stream waters bring tropical influences northward. Look for them around underwater structures, drop-offs, and areas where baitfish concentrate.

seasonality.spring: Northern sennets begin arriving in New England waters as temperatures warm, following schools of baitfish northward from their southern wintering grounds.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for northern sennets, when they're most active and numerous in our waters, actively feeding and easiest to catch from boats in deeper offshore areas.
seasonality.fall: Still present but beginning their southward migration as water temperatures drop, often found closer to shore during this transition period.
seasonality.winter: Absent from New England waters, having migrated south to warmer Atlantic waters where they spend the coldest months.

funFact: Despite being a barracuda, northern sennets are so rarely eaten that most fishing guides recommend releasing them - not because they're bad tasting, but because they're considered much more valuable as exciting gamefish that put up spectacular fights when hooked!
confusionNotes: Northern sennets are most easily confused with needlefish, but sennets have a much more robust, muscular body and two separate dorsal fins, while needlefish are extremely thin with a single dorsal fin. Remember: sennets are built like torpedoes, needlefish like needles.
contextualKnowledge: Many anglers are surprised to catch a 'barracuda' in New England waters, as most people associate these fish exclusively with tropical destinations like Florida or the Caribbean. The northern sennet proves that some tropical species do venture into our cooler waters during summer months.
compareHints: As the only barracuda species regularly found in New England, northern sennets are unique in our waters. Compared to their tropical barracuda cousins like the great barracuda, northern sennets are much smaller and more tolerant of cooler water temperatures. They share the family's characteristic torpedo shape and sharp teeth but lack the size and aggressive reputation of their southern relatives.
